claim: Axolotls are unique in their ability to regenerate the spinal cord.
source: Axolotls are unique in their ability to regenerate the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a statement presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, drawing on established knowledge about axolotl regenerative capabilities.

claim: Regenerating stem cells in the axolotl spinal cord revert to a molecular state resembling embryonic neuroepithelial cells.
source: Previously, we showed that regenerating stem cells in the axolotl spinal cord revert to a molecular state resembling embryonic neuroepithelial cells and functionally acquire rapid proliferative divisions (Rodrigo Albors et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Regenerating stem cells in the axolotl spinal cord functionally acquire rapid proliferative divisions.
source: Previously, we showed that regenerating stem cells in the axolotl spinal cord revert to a molecular state resembling embryonic neuroepithelial cells and functionally acquire rapid proliferative divisions (Rodrigo Albors et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: A high-proliferation zone exists in the regenerating spinal cord that shifts posteriorly over time.
source: Here, we refine the analysis of cell proliferation in space and time and identify a high-proliferation zone in the regenerating spinal cord that shifts posteriorly over time.
evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial analysis of proliferation markers presented in the manuscript.

claim: The acceleration of the cell cycle is the major driver of regenerative spinal cord outgrowth in axolotls.
source: Our model shows that while cell influx and neural stem cell activation play a minor role, the acceleration of the cell cycle is the major driver of regenerative spinal cord outgrowth in axolotls.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling that integrates multiple quantitative datasets and tests different scenarios.

claim: Cell influx plays a minor role in regenerative spinal cord outgrowth in axolotls.
source: Our model shows that while cell influx and neural stem cell activation play a minor role, the acceleration of the cell cycle is the major driver of regenerative spinal cord outgrowth in axolotls.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling comparing different cellular mechanisms.

claim: Neural stem cell activation plays a minor role in regenerative spinal cord outgrowth in axolotls.
source: Our model shows that while cell influx and neural stem cell activation play a minor role, the acceleration of the cell cycle is the major driver of regenerative spinal cord outgrowth in axolotls.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling comparing different cellular mechanisms.

claim: Only in salamanders are neural stem cells mobilized efficiently to resolve spinal cord injuries.
source: Neural stem cells exist in the spinal cord of all vertebrates, but only in salamanders these cells are mobilized efficiently to resolve spinal cord injuries (Becker and Becker, 2015; Tanaka and Ferretti, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neural stem cells exist in the spinal cord of all vertebrates.
source: Neural stem cells exist in the spinal cord of all vertebrates, but only in salamanders these cells are mobilized efficiently to resolve spinal cord injuries (Becker and Becker, 2015; Tanaka and Ferretti, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Cells adjacent to the cut end regrow a fully functional spinal cord following tail amputation in axolotls.
source: In axolotls, this is best exemplified following tail amputation, when cells adjacent to the cut end regrow a fully functional spinal cord (Holtzer, 1956; Mchedlishvili et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Resident SOX2+ neural stem cells re-activate an embryonic-like gene expression program following tail amputation.
source: There, we found that resident SOX2+ neural stem cells re-activate an embryonic-like gene expression program following tail amputation (Rodrigo Albors et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The embryonic-like gene expression program involves the re-establishment of planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling.
source: Part of this program involves the re-establishment of planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling, the downregulation of pro-neural genes, and upregulation of proliferation-promoting genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors in the preceding sentence.

claim: The embryonic-like gene expression program involves the downregulation of pro-neural genes.
source: Part of this program involves the re-establishment of planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling, the downregulation of pro-neural genes, and upregulation of proliferation-promoting genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors in the preceding sentence.

claim: The embryonic-like gene expression program involves upregulation of proliferation-promoting genes.
source: Part of this program involves the re-establishment of planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling, the downregulation of pro-neural genes, and upregulation of proliferation-promoting genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors in the preceding sentence.

claim: Regenerating neural stem cells speed up their cell cycle.
source: In line with these gene expression changes, we also found that regenerating neural stem cells speed up their cell cycle, and switch from neuron-generating to proliferative cell divisions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors in the preceding context.

claim: Regenerating neural stem cells switch from neuron-generating to proliferative cell divisions.
source: In line with these gene expression changes, we also found that regenerating neural stem cells speed up their cell cycle, and switch from neuron-generating to proliferative cell divisions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors in the preceding context.

claim: PCP is key for the efficient and orderly expansion of the regenerating spinal cord.
source: PCP turned out to be key for the efficient and orderly expansion of the regenerating spinal cord, at least in part by instructing cells to divide along the growing axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors in the preceding context.

claim: PCP instructs cells to divide along the growing axis.
source: PCP turned out to be key for the efficient and orderly expansion of the regenerating spinal cord, at least in part by instructing cells to divide along the growing axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors in the preceding context.

claim: The regenerating spinal cord initially extended slowly to a mean outgrowth of 0.45 ± 0.04 mm at day 4.
source: Initially, the regenerating spinal cord extended slowly to a mean outgrowth of 0.45 ± 0.04 mm at day 4 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The spinal cord reached an outgrowth of 2.26 ± 0.07 mm by day 8.
source: Thereafter, the spinal cord grew faster, reaching an outgrowth of 2.26 ± 0.07 mm by day 8.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements referenced in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The number of SOX2+ cells per spinal cord cross section is constant along the AP axis in both uninjured and regenerating samples at any time.
source: We found that the number of SOX2+ cells per spinal cord cross section is constant along the AP axis in both uninjured and regenerating samples at any time (Figure 2B,B' and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cell counts shown in figures.

claim: The number of SOX2+ cells per cross section spatially averaged along the AP axis is constant during regeneration.
source: We also found that the number of SOX2+ cells per cross section spatially averaged along the AP axis is constant during regeneration (Figure 2C and see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: On average, 30.4 ± 0.6 SOX2+ cells make up the circumference of the axolotl spinal cord.
source: On average, 30.4 ± 0.6 SOX2+ cells make up the circumference of the axolotl spinal cord.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from the data.

claim: The length of SOX2+ cells along the AP axis does not change during regeneration (lc = 13.2 ± 0.1 μm).
source: Since the length of SOX2+ cells along the AP axis does not change during regeneration (lc = 13.2 ± 0.1 μm) (Rodrigo Albors et al., 2015), the density of cells along the AP axis is spatially homogeneous and equal to 2.3 ± 0.6 cells/μm (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The density of cells along the AP axis is spatially homogeneous and equal to 2.3 ± 0.6 cells/μm.
source: Since the length of SOX2+ cells along the AP axis does not change during regeneration (lc = 13.2 ± 0.1 μm) (Rodrigo Albors et al., 2015), the density of cells along the AP axis is spatially homogeneous and equal to 2.3 ± 0.6 cells/μm (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is derived from measurements of cell number and cell length.

claim: Convergence and extension are not driving forces of regenerative spinal cord outgrowth in the axolotl.
source: Taken together, these findings allow us to exclude mechanisms such as cell shape changes and convergence and extension as driving forces of regenerative spinal cord outgrowth in the axolotl.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the finding that cell density remains constant.

claim: Cell shape changes are not driving forces of regenerative spinal cord outgrowth in the axolotl.
source: Taken together, these findings allow us to exclude mechanisms such as cell shape changes and convergence and extension as driving forces of regenerative spinal cord outgrowth in the axolotl.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the finding that cell density remains constant.

claim: Constant neural stem cell density implies an increasing neural stem cell number during regeneration.
source: Instead, constant neural stem cell density implies an increasing neural stem cell number during regeneration.
evidence: This is a logical inference from constant density and increasing tissue length.

claim: The expansion of the regenerating neural stem cell pool mostly relies on proliferation-based mechanisms.
source: This suggests that the expansion of the regenerating neural stem cell pool mostly relies on proliferation-based mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the exclusion of other mechanisms and the observation of increasing cell numbers.

claim: A high-proliferation zone emerges in the regenerating spinal cord at day 4.
source: These findings reveal that a high-proliferation zone emerges in the regenerating spinal cord at day 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial analysis of proliferation markers showing significant differences between zones from day 4 onward.

claim: At day 4, the switchpoint between the two zones is located 800 ± 100 μm anterior to the amputation plane.
source: At this time point, the switchpoint between the two zones is located 800 ± 100 μm anterior to the amputation plane, but shows the tendency to shift posteriorly as the regenerating spinal cord grows (Figure 2F'').
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting to experimental data shown in Figure 2F''.

claim: The switchpoint shows the tendency to shift posteriorly as the regenerating spinal cord grows.
source: At this time point, the switchpoint between the two zones is located 800 ± 100 μm anterior to the amputation plane, but shows the tendency to shift posteriorly as the regenerating spinal cord grows (Figure 2F'').
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting to experimental data shown in Figure 2F''.

claim: The proliferation rate is 0.06 ± 0.02 per day in the uninjured spinal cord.
source: We find that the proliferation rate is 0.06 ± 0.02 per day in the uninjured spinal cord which corresponds to a cell cycle length of 10 ± 4 days (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by calculations from mitotic index and cell cycle length measurements.

claim: The proliferation rate in the uninjured spinal cord corresponds to a cell cycle length of 10 ± 4 days.
source: We find that the proliferation rate is 0.06 ± 0.02 per day in the uninjured spinal cord which corresponds to a cell cycle length of 10 ± 4 days (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is derived from proliferation rate measurements.

claim: At day 4 the proliferation rate increases to about 0.15 per day corresponding to a cell cycle length of about five days.
source: However, at day 4 the proliferation rate increases to about 0.15 per day corresponding to a cell cycle length of about five days and the proliferation rate remains that high until day 8.
evidence: This claim is supported by calculations from mitotic index and cell cycle length measurements.

claim: The proliferation rate remains high until day 8.
source: However, at day 4 the proliferation rate increases to about 0.15 per day corresponding to a cell cycle length of about five days and the proliferation rate remains that high until day 8.
evidence: This claim is supported by calculations from mitotic index and cell cycle length measurements.

claim: The number of SOX2+/PCNA- cells drops from 180 ± 30 at day 0 to 23 ± 13 at day 6.
source: The number of SOX2+/PCNA- cells drops from 180 ± 30 at day 0 to 23 ± 13 at day 6 (Figure 2H) which suggests that quiescent SOX2+ cells get activated and re-enter the cell cycle upon injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Quiescent SOX2+ cells get activated and re-enter the cell cycle upon injury.
source: The number of SOX2+/PCNA- cells drops from 180 ± 30 at day 0 to 23 ± 13 at day 6 (Figure 2H) which suggests that quiescent SOX2+ cells get activated and re-enter the cell cycle upon injury.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the decrease in quiescent cell numbers.

claim: The number of quiescent SOX2+ cells appears to increase again at day 8, when cells resume neurogenesis.
source: The number of quiescent SOX2+ cells appears to increase again at day 8, when cells resume neurogenesis (Rodrigo Albors et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data and citation to prior work.

claim: Labelled cells preserve their original spatial order during regeneration.
source: We found that labelled cells preserve their original spatial order: cells located close to the amputation plane end up at the posterior end of the regenerated spinal cord (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by clone tracking experiments shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Cells located close to the amputation plane end up at the posterior end of the regenerated spinal cord.
source: We found that labelled cells preserve their original spatial order: cells located close to the amputation plane end up at the posterior end of the regenerated spinal cord (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by clone tracking experiments shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Most-anterior cells almost do not change their position during regeneration.
source: Most-anterior cells, however, almost do not change their position.
evidence: This claim is supported by clone tracking experiments.

claim: Clones initially located 800 μm anterior to the amputation plane translocate slowly, with a velocity of 20 ± 9 μm/day.
source: Clones initially located 800 μm anterior to the amputation plane translocate slowly, with a velocity of 20 ± 9 μm/day.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of clone trajectories shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The more posterior a clone is, the faster it translocates.
source: In contrast, the more posterior a clone is, the faster it translocates (Figure 2K).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of clone velocities shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The spinal cord must grow as a result of increasing cell numbers.
source: The fact that cell density along the AP axis is constant in space and time (Figure 2B–C) made us reason that the spinal cord must grow as a result of increasing cell numbers.
evidence: This is a logical inference from constant cell density and increasing tissue length.

claim: The increase in cell proliferation is due to both the acceleration of the cell cycle and the activation of quiescent stem cells.
source: In line with this, we found a high-proliferation zone, first spanning from 800 μm anterior to the amputation plane, and showed that the increase in cell proliferation is due to both (i) the acceleration of the cell cycle and (ii) the activation of quiescent stem cells (Figure 2D–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental measurements and analyses shown in Figure 2D-H.

claim: The model prediction of spinal cord outgrowth is in agreement with experimental data.
source: Importantly, the model predicts a spinal cord outgrowth time-course that recapitulates the observed experimental data (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The acceleration of the cell cycle, the activation of quiescent neural stem cells, and an influx of cells into the regenerate quantitatively explain the observed spinal cord outgrowth.
source: This fit-free agreement shows that the acceleration of the cell cycle, the activation of quiescent neural stem cells, and an influx of cells into the regenerate quantitatively explain the observed spinal cord outgrowth.
evidence: This claim is supported by the agreement between model predictions and experimental data.

claim: Switching off the acceleration of the cell cycle predicted a maximum outgrowth of 1.7 mm (p=0.003) which is 0.6 mm shorter than the observed outgrowth at day 8.
source: First, we switched off the acceleration of the cell cycle, modeling growth only with basal cell proliferation, the influx of cells, and the activation of quiescent neural stem cells (Figure 3D). This predicted a maximum outgrowth of 1.7 mm (p=0.003) which is 0.6 mm shorter than the observed outgrowth at day 8.
evidence: This claim is supported by in silico modeling experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The acceleration of the cell cycle is a key driver of regenerative spinal cord outgrowth.
source: This result shows that the acceleration of the cell cycle is a key driver of regenerative spinal cord outgrowth.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the modeling results showing significant reduction in outgrowth when cell cycle acceleration is removed.

claim: Switching off cell influx has almost no effect on the predicted outgrowth.
source: In contrast, switching off cell influx (Figure 3E) or the activation of quiescent neural stem cells (Figure 3F) has almost no effect on the predicted outgrowth, which suggests that these cellular mechanisms are not major drivers of regenerative spinal cord outgrowth.
evidence: This claim is supported by in silico modeling experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Switching off the activation of quiescent neural stem cells has almost no effect on the predicted outgrowth.
source: In contrast, switching off cell influx (Figure 3E) or the activation of quiescent neural stem cells (Figure 3F) has almost no effect on the predicted outgrowth, which suggests that these cellular mechanisms are not major drivers of regenerative spinal cord outgrowth.
evidence: This claim is supported by in silico modeling experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Cell influx and activation of quiescent neural stem cells are not major drivers of regenerative spinal cord outgrowth.
source: In contrast, switching off cell influx (Figure 3E) or the activation of quiescent neural stem cells (Figure 3F) has almost no effect on the predicted outgrowth, which suggests that these cellular mechanisms are not major drivers of regenerative spinal cord outgrowth.
evidence: This claim is inferred from modeling results showing minimal effect when these mechanisms are removed.

claim: The acceleration of the cell cycle in cells that were already proliferating in the uninjured spinal cord can explain the observed spinal cord outgrowth during regeneration.
source: Together, these results show that the acceleration of the cell cycle in cells that were already proliferating in the uninjured spinal cord can explain the observed spinal cord outgrowth during regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results showing that cell cycle acceleration alone is sufficient to explain outgrowth.

claim: Sox2-knockout prevented the acceleration of the cell cycle during regeneration.
source: Fei and colleagues found evidences that Sox2-knockout prevented the acceleration of the cell cycle during regeneration and lead to shorter spinal cord outgrowth.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to work by Fei et al., 2014.

claim: Sox2-knockout lead to shorter spinal cord outgrowth.
source: Fei and colleagues found evidences that Sox2-knockout prevented the acceleration of the cell cycle during regeneration and lead to shorter spinal cord outgrowth.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to work by Fei et al., 2014.

claim: Running the model with the acceleration of the cell cycle switched off recapitulated the shorter outgrowth in the Sox2-knockout condition.
source: In agreement with these findings, running our model with the acceleration of the cell cycle switched off recapitulated the shorter outgrowth in the Sox2-knockout condition (Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by model predictions compared to independent experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increased proliferation of SOX2+ cells upon spinal cord injury is a common feature among vertebrates.
source: Increased proliferation of SOX2+ cells upon spinal cord injury is a common feature among vertebrates (Becker and Becker, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In zebrafish, Xenopus, mouse and axolotl traumatic spinal cord injury triggers a long-range wave of increased cell proliferation.
source: In zebrafish (Hui et al., 2010, 2015), Xenopus (Gaete et al., 2012), mouse (Lacroix et al., 2014) and axolotl (this work, Rodrigo Albors et al., 2015; Holtzer, 1956) traumatic spinal cord injury triggers a long-range wave of increased cell proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies and data from this work.

claim: Although the potential to replace lost cells or tissue exists in other species, they are not as efficient as axolotls at resolving spinal cord injuries.
source: It is however clear that although the potential to replace lost cells or tissue exists in other species, they are not as efficient as axolotls at resolving spinal cord injuries.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Spinal cord stem cells in the axolotl speed up their cell cycle during regeneration.
source: In our previous study, we uncovered that spinal cord stem cells in the axolotl speed up their cell cycle during regeneration (Rodrigo Albors et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The high-proliferation zone initially spans from the 800 μm adjacent to the amputation plane to the regenerating tip.
source: Performing detailed quantifications, we were now able to delineate a high-proliferation zone that initially spans from the 800 μm adjacent to the amputation plane to the regenerating tip, and later shifts posteriorly as the spinal cord regrows.
evidence: This claim is supported by detailed quantitative analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The high-proliferation zone later shifts posteriorly as the spinal cord regrows.
source: Performing detailed quantifications, we were now able to delineate a high-proliferation zone that initially spans from the 800 μm adjacent to the amputation plane to the regenerating tip, and later shifts posteriorly as the spinal cord regrows.
evidence: This claim is supported by detailed quantitative analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The observed increase in proliferation is primarily due to the acceleration of the cell cycle within the regenerating neural stem cell pool.
source: Although some quiescent neural stem cells enter the cell cycle during regeneration, we demonstrate that the observed increase in proliferation is primarily due to the acceleration of the cell cycle within the regenerating neural stem cell pool.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis and modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: The acceleration of the cell cycle can explain the observed spinal cord outgrowth.
source: By performing experiments in silico using our mechanistic model of spinal cord regeneration, we demonstrate that the acceleration of the cell cycle can explain the observed spinal cord outgrowth.
evidence: This claim is supported by in silico modeling experiments.

claim: Sox2-knockout spinal cords do not regrow properly upon amputation, due to the inability of Sox2-knockout cells to 'change gears' in response to injury.
source: We further applied our model to an independent experimental dataset in which Sox2-knockout spinal cords do not regrow properly upon amputation, due to the inability of Sox2-knockout cells to 'change gears' in response to injury (Fei et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to work by Fei et al., 2014.

claim: Sox2-knockout cells express PCNA and are in theory able to proliferate.
source: Indeed, Sox2-knockout cells express PCNA and are in theory able to proliferate, but their lower incorporation of the thymidine analog 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) suggests that they cannot speed up the cell cycle (Fei et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to work by Fei et al., 2014.

claim: Sox2-knockout cells' lower incorporation of EdU suggests that they cannot speed up the cell cycle.
source: Indeed, Sox2-knockout cells express PCNA and are in theory able to proliferate, but their lower incorporation of the thymidine analog 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) suggests that they cannot speed up the cell cycle (Fei et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to work by Fei et al., 2014.

claim: The reduced outgrowth in Sox2-knockout spinal cords can be quantitatively explained by the lack of cell cycle acceleration.
source: We were able to show that the reduced outgrowth in Sox2-knockout spinal cords can be quantitatively explained by the lack of cell cycle acceleration (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by model predictions compared to experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cells initially located within the 500 μm anterior to the amputation plane contribute to the regenerated spinal cord.
source: In line with earlier work (Mchedlishvili et al., 2007), we found that cells initially located within the 500 μm anterior to the amputation plane contribute to the regenerated spinal cord; while cells outside this zone translocate slower, and cells at 800 μm, the border of the high-proliferation zone, almost do not move.
evidence: This claim is supported by clone tracking data and citation to prior work.

claim: Cells outside the 500 μm zone anterior to the amputation plane translocate slower.
source: In line with earlier work (Mchedlishvili et al., 2007), we found that cells initially located within the 500 μm anterior to the amputation plane contribute to the regenerated spinal cord; while cells outside this zone translocate slower, and cells at 800 μm, the border of the high-proliferation zone, almost do not move.
evidence: This claim is supported by clone tracking data.

claim: Cells at 800 μm, the border of the high-proliferation zone, almost do not move.
source: In line with earlier work (Mchedlishvili et al., 2007), we found that cells initially located within the 500 μm anterior to the amputation plane contribute to the regenerated spinal cord; while cells outside this zone translocate slower, and cells at 800 μm, the border of the high-proliferation zone, almost do not move.
evidence: This claim is supported by clone tracking data.

claim: Cells are passively displaced, pushed by more anterior dividing cells.
source: This would be consistent with a model in which cells are passively displaced, pushed by more anterior dividing cells.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the observed cell movement patterns.

claim: The more posterior a cell is the more cells anterior to that cell divide and the stronger is the push, making the cell translocate faster.
source: In this model, the more posterior a cell is the more cells anterior to that cell divide and the stronger is the push, making the cell translocate faster (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed velocity gradient.

claim: The proliferative response extends beyond the 500 μm anterior to the amputation plane that gives rise to the regenerated spinal cord.
source: Importantly, the proliferative response extends beyond the 500 μm anterior to the amputation plane that gives rise to the regenerated spinal cord (Mchedlishvili et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cells in the posterior 500 μm of the high-proliferation zone regenerate the spinal cord while cells from the anterior 300 μm of the high-proliferation zone replenish and push out the 500 μm regeneration source zone.
source: In the light of this model, it is plausible that cells in the posterior 500 μm of the high-proliferation zone regenerate the spinal cord while cells from the anterior 300 μm of the high-proliferation zone replenish and push out the 500 μm regeneration source zone.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The increase in cell numbers during regeneration is tightly regulated so that the regenerating spinal cord extends while maintaining constant cell density and proper tube-like structure.
source: A notable finding of this study is that the increase in cell numbers during regeneration is tightly regulated so that the regenerating spinal cord extends while maintaining constant cell density and proper tube-like structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation of constant cell density during outgrowth.

claim: The tube-like structure made up almost entirely of neural stem cells might be essential to act as a scaffold for rebuilding the spinal cord tissue architecture.
source: This tube-like structure made up almost entirely of neural stem cells might be essential to act as a scaffold for rebuilding the spinal cord tissue architecture.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed structure.

claim: The activation of PCP signaling within the source zone instructs cells to divide along the growing axis of the spinal cord and is key for effective spinal cord regeneration.
source: Previously, we showed that the activation of PCP signaling within the source zone instructs cells to divide along the growing axis of the spinal cord and is key for effective spinal cord regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to prior work by the authors.

claim: Orderly and directed expansion of the neural stem cell pool is important for efficient spinal cord regeneration.
source: This work highlights the importance of orderly and directed expansion of the neural stem cell pool for efficient spinal cord regeneration.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Axolotl spinal cord outgrowth is driven by the acceleration of the cell cycle in a pool of SOX2+ neural stem cells restricted in space and time.
source: Together, our findings provide a quantitative mechanistic understanding of the cellular mechanisms that drive complete spinal cord regeneration in axolotls. By performing a quantitative modeling approach combined with quantitative experimental data, we found that axolotl spinal cord outgrowth is driven by the acceleration of the cell cycle in a pool of SOX2+ neural stem cells restricted in space and time.
evidence: This claim is supported by the integrated analysis of experimental data and mathematical modeling.

claim: The cell cycle length at day six was estimated as 117 ± 12 hours corresponding to a proliferation rate of 0.21 ± 0.02 per day.
source: For the sake of consistent methodology within the present study, the data were reanalyzed with bootstrapping using case resampling (see 'brdu_bootstrapping_day6' in Rost et al., 2016a). In agreement with the previous analysis the cell cycle length was estimated as 117 ± 12 hours corresponding to a proliferation rate of 0.21 ± 0.02 per day at six days after amputation.
evidence: This claim is supported by reanalysis of BrdU labeling data.

claim: The regenerating spinal cord grew faster after day 4.
source: Initially, the regenerating spinal cord extended slowly to a mean outgrowth of 0.45 ± 0.04 mm at day 4 (Figure 1B). Thereafter, the spinal cord grew faster, reaching an outgrowth of 2.26 ± 0.07 mm by day 8.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of outgrowth rates before and after day 4.

claim: The growth fraction and mitotic index are not significantly different between the two modeled zones in the uninjured spinal cord.
source: Not surprisingly, we found that in the uninjured spinal cord the growth fraction and the mitotic index in the two modeled zones are not significantly different (Figure 2D,F,F' and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting to experimental data.

claim: At day 3 there are no significant differences between the two zones in growth fraction and mitotic index.
source: Similarly, at day 3 there are no significant differences between the two zones (Figure 2F,F' and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting to experimental data.

claim: The growth fraction and the mitotic index are higher in the posterior zone from day 4 onward.
source: In contrast, the growth fraction and the mitotic index are higher in the posterior zone from day 4 onward (Figure 2D',F,F' and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting to experimental data.

claim: The model successfully recapitulated the experimental outgrowth in the Sox2-knockout scenario.
source: The fact that the model successfully recapitulated the experimental outgrowth in the Sox2-knockout scenario suggests that compensatory mechanisms might have a small contribution in this condition.
evidence: This claim is based on the agreement between model predictions and experimental data for Sox2-knockout.

claim: Compensatory mechanisms might have a small contribution in the Sox2-knockout condition.
source: The fact that the model successfully recapitulated the experimental outgrowth in the Sox2-knockout scenario suggests that compensatory mechanisms might have a small contribution in this condition.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on model predictions.

claim: The cell cycle entry rate k = 0.2 ± 0.1 day−1.
source: By fitting the model to the experimental growth fraction data from day 0 to day 6 (Figure 3B), we determined this parameter as k = 0.2 ± 0.1 day−1.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting to experimental data.

claim: Even when both cell influx and cell activation are switched off, the observed outgrowth time-course is in agreement with the model prediction.
source: Indeed, even when we switched off both cell influx and cell activation the observed outgrowth time-course is in agreement with the model prediction (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in silico modeling experiments shown in Figure 3G.
